newsitem.title: BOSNIA: End to US/Bosnian row over defence aide unclear.
newsitem.headline: End to US/Bosnian row over defence aide unclear.

text.p: Bosnian and U.S. officials on Sunday declined to comment directly on a dispute over Washington's demand for the removal of a Sarajevo defence official with alleged ties to Iran.
But a Bosnian government official hinted at a possible quiet resolution to the disagreement which has held up the delivery of U.S. arms to the Moslem-Croat federation.
"The (Moslem-Croat) federation assembly is due to convene at the end of October and it will appoint ministers of the new government," said a Bosnian government official, who asked not to be named.
The official implied a face-saving solution might be for deputy defence minister Hasan Cengic to lose his current job in an official reshuffle.
"If the current dispute can be resolved like this, that would be the best solution to lower the tensions," the official said.
Sarajevo has so far failed to sack Cengic, and a ship carrying the bulk of a $100 million arms shipment for the federation army has sailed away from Croatia unloaded.
The arms are part of the U.S.-backed "Train and Equip" programme, and the United States says they will not be delivered until Cengic is removed from his post.
It was unclear whether Washington would be satisfied if Cengic were shifted to another job outside the defence ministry.
A statement from the office of Moslem president Alija Izetbegovic on Saturday denied the defence official's reported links to Iran were behind a U.S. demand for his removal.
Izetbegovic's office said that Washington had accused Cengic of failing to cooperate in drawing up and carrying out the defence law for the joint federation army.
It also said a similar request had been made by Washington to dismiss a Croat defence minister. Cengic is his deputy.
There has been considerable reluctance from both Moslems and Croats, who fought an 11-month war in 1993, to merging their forces in one army.
The defence law, adopted under U.S. pressure earlier this year, created a joint command structure but failed to merge the the forces completely.

Washington has said openly that disputes relating to the implementation of the troublesome defence law needed to be resolved before the shipment was unloaded and transported to federation storage sites.
Cengic was apparently still in his office on Saturday, receiving a military delegation from Turkey.
U.S. embassy officials in Sarajevo on Sunday declined to comment on the matter.
James Pardew, the American envoy in charge of the military aid programme expressed optimism earlier in the weekend that the issue would be settled soon.
